title: Algebra I — Common Core High School Math — Answer Key
id_format: S<set>-<section>-Q<number>; section is M (main), B1, B2, ... (backward), F1 or F2 (forward)
grading_rules: Match each student response to its key record by the question ID printed on the question page (for example S40-F2-Q3). The page number is the same in the Question Collection and the Answer Key. IDs are unique within one grade's collection; across collections use uid (for example G5:S40-F2-Q3).
Multiple choice and true/false: the response is correct when the chosen letter equals correct_letter, or when the student wrote the text of the correct choice.

Short answer: accept any mathematically equivalent form unless the question asks for a specific form (equivalent fractions, decimals, and mixed numbers; a ratio written as a : b, a to b, or a/b; "x = 5" or "5"; terms of an expression in any order). Units are not required unless the question asks for them.
When an answer has several parts (separated by semicolons, or with labels such as "Rate of change:"), every part must be correct.
Drawing / plotting questions (type plot): correct_answer describes what a correct drawing shows. Judge the student's drawing against it.

Drawing + written questions (type plot_text): the student draws on the figure AND writes an answer. drawing_answer describes the correct drawing and correct_answer the written answer. Both must be correct: every requested point, segment or shape in the drawing, and the written conclusion.

Answer with required work (type work): required_method says what the shown work must use. A correct final answer without that work earns partial credit only; correct work with a slip in the final answer is also partial.
Explain / describe questions: grading_note says what a correct response must include; accept any reasonable wording.
grading_note also lists other accepted answers and the work behind an answer. It is guidance for the grader, not for students.

Algebra I answer forms: the grading_note of every written answer begins with "Form required:" or with "Any" (for example "Any equivalent form", "Any equivalent wording", or "Any correct graph"), which says what else is accepted. When a form is required (for example expanded, factored completely, simplest radical form, slope-intercept form, vertex form, exact value, or a stated rounding), an answer in another form is not full credit even if it is equivalent.

Equations, inequalities, and systems: "x = 3" and "3" are the same answer; a solution set must contain every solution (both roots of a quadratic, in any order); "no solution" and "all real numbers" are answers when the key says so; an inequality may be written either way round (x > 2 or 2 < x) unless a notation is asked for; a solution of a system may be written as an ordered pair or as x = ..., y = ....
Every question has an explanation in its grading_note, after the form rule. It shows why the key is correct and can be shown to the student as feedback after grading.

questions.set_title: Prove that the sum of a rational number and an irrational number is irrational
questions.section_title: Algebra I main question
questions.domain: Number & Quantity: The Real Number System
questions.question: Explain why 5 + √2 is irrational. (Suppose 5 + √2 = r for some rational number r.)
questions.required_method: An argument like this: if 5 + √2 = r with r rational, then √2 = r - 5, a difference of rational numbers, which is rational. But √2 is irrational, so 5 + √2 cannot be rational.
questions.grading_note: Any equivalent form of the argument. The key step is that rational numbers are closed under subtraction.

questions.set_title: Prove that the sum of a rational number and an irrational number is irrational
questions.section_title: Algebra I main question
questions.domain: Number & Quantity: The Real Number System
questions.question: Explain why √3 - 4 is irrational. (Suppose √3 - 4 = r for some rational number r.)
questions.required_method: An argument like this: if √3 - 4 = r with r rational, then √3 = r + 4, a sum of rational numbers, which is rational. But √3 is irrational, so √3 - 4 cannot be rational.
questions.grading_note: Form required: the argument by contradiction. It must use the fact that a sum of rational numbers is rational.

questions.set_title: Prove that the sum of a rational number and an irrational number is irrational
questions.section_title: Algebra I main question
questions.domain: Number & Quantity: The Real Number System
questions.question: Prove that if a is rational and x is irrational, then a + x is irrational.
questions.required_method: Suppose a + x = r with r rational. Then x = r - a, a difference of rational numbers, which is rational. That contradicts x being irrational, so a + x is irrational.
questions.grading_note: Form required: the general argument by contradiction, using closure of the rational numbers under subtraction.

questions.set_title: Choose a level of accuracy that fits the limits of measurement

questions.question: A gym charges C = 35 + 20m dollars for m months of membership. What do 35 and 20 represent?

questions.grading_note: Any equivalent wording. Both meanings are required.

questions.set_title: Interpret the terms, factors, and coefficients of an expression in context

questions.question: The expression 1.08p gives the total cost, including sales tax, of an item with price p. What does the factor 1.08 tell you?
questions.correct_answer: The total is 108% of the price: the price plus 8% tax (1.08p = p + 0.08p).
questions.grading_note: Any equivalent wording that names the 8% tax.

questions.grading_note: 2(l + w) is two copies of (l + w), so (l + w) is half of the perimeter.

questions.set_title: Interpret the terms, factors, and coefficients of an expression in context
questions.section_title: Algebra I main question
questions.question: For the expression 3x² - 5x + 7, name its terms, the coefficient of x, and the constant term.
questions.correct_answer: Terms: 3x², -5x, and 7; the coefficient of x is -5; the constant term is 7.
questions.grading_note: Any equivalent form. All three parts are required. The sign belongs to the term: the x-term is -5x.

questions.set_title: Interpret the terms, factors, and coefficients of an expression in context
questions.section_title: Algebra I main question
questions.question: A car's value is 500(0.9)^t dollars after t years. The factor 0.9 means the car loses 90% of its value each year.
questions.grading_note: Multiplying by 0.9 keeps 90% of the value each year, so the car loses 10% each year.

questions.question: What is the coefficient of y in 7y - 2?

questions.grading_note: Form required: the x-value, the greatest value, and the reason.

questions.question: Derive the quadratic formula. Start from ax² + bx + c = 0 with a ≠ 0, and complete the square to solve for x.
questions.required_method: Every step shown: divide by a; subtract c ÷ a; add (b ÷ (2a))² to both sides; write (x + b ÷ (2a))² = (b² - 4ac) ÷ (4a²); take square roots, using ±; subtract b ÷ (2a).

questions.correct_answer: Add b² ÷ (4a²); the left side becomes (x + b ÷ (2a))².
questions.required_method: Half of the x-coefficient, b ÷ (2a), squared: (b ÷ (2a))² = b² ÷ (4a²); then the left side factored as a square.
questions.grading_note: Form required: the number added and the squared binomial.

questions.set_title: Derive the quadratic formula by completing the square

questions.correct_answer: Both the positive and the negative square roots of the right side work, so x + b ÷ (2a) = ±√(b² - 4ac) ÷ √(4a²). √(4a²) = 2|a|, and the ± already covers both signs, so the denominator can be written 2a.

questions.set_title: Show that replacing an equation by its sum with a multiple of the other keeps the solutions of a system
questions.section_title: Algebra I main question
questions.question: System: x + y = 7 and x - y = 1. Replace the second equation by the sum of the two equations. Write the new system, solve it, and show that the solution also satisfies the original system.
questions.required_method: The new system x + y = 7 and 2x = 8, its solution, and a check of the solution in both original equations.
questions.grading_note: Form required: the new system, the solution, and the check. 2x = 8 gives x = 4, so y = 3. Check: 4 + 3 = 7 and 4 - 3 = 1.

questions.set_title: Show that replacing an equation by its sum with a multiple of the other keeps the solutions of a system
questions.section_title: Algebra I main question
questions.question: Suppose (a, b) is a solution of the system 2x + y = 5 and x - 3y = 6. Explain why (a, b) is also a solution of (2x + y) + 2(x - 3y) = 5 + 2(6).
questions.correct_answer: Since 2a + b = 5 and a - 3b = 6, 2(a - 3b) = 12. Adding equal amounts to both sides of 2a + b = 5 gives (2a + b) + 2(a - 3b) = 5 + 12, a true equation.
questions.grading_note: Any equivalent explanation that substitutes (a, b) and adds equal quantities to both sides.

questions.question: System: 3x + 2y = 12 and x - y = -1. Which system has the same solution?
questions.grading_note: Adding the first equation and 2 times the second gives 5x = 10. The solution of both systems is (2, 3); (2, 3) does not satisfy 5x = 14, 4x + y = 13, or 2x + 3y = 11.

questions.grading_note: Any solution of the old system satisfies the new equation, and the old equation can be recovered by subtracting 3 times the other, so the solutions stay the same.

questions.section_title: Algebra I main question
questions.question: System A: x + 2y = 7 and 3x - y = 7. System B: x + 2y = 7 and 7x = 21, where 7x = 21 is the first equation plus 2 times the second. Show that every solution of A solves B and every solution of B solves A. Then give the solution.
questions.required_method: A to B: a solution of A makes both equations true, so adding x + 2y = 7 and 2(3x - y) = 14 gives 7x = 21. B to A: from 7x = 21 and x + 2y = 7, subtracting gives 6x - 2y = 14, so 3x - y = 7. The kept equation x + 2y = 7 is in both systems.
questions.grading_note: Form required: both directions and the solution. Check: 3 + 4 = 7 and 9 - 2 = 7.

questions.set_title: Prove that replacing an equation by its sum with a multiple of the other gives an equivalent system, in both directions
questions.section_title: Algebra I main question
questions.question: Let P = c and Q = d be the two equations of a system (P and Q are expressions in x and y). Prove that the system P = c and Q + kP = d + kc has exactly the same solutions, for any number k.
questions.correct_answer: The two systems have the same solutions.
questions.required_method: If (x, y) makes P = c and Q = d true, then Q + kP = d + kc (adding equal amounts), so it solves the new system. Conversely, if P = c and Q + kP = d + kc, subtracting kP = kc gives Q = d. So the solution sets are equal.
questions.grading_note: Form required: both directions, each with its reason.

questions.set_title: Prove that replacing an equation by its sum with a multiple of the other gives an equivalent system, in both directions

questions.correct_answer: The kept equation is needed to recover the replaced one. For example, replacing both x + y = 2 and x - y = 0 with their sum 2x = 2 alone loses information: 2x = 2 has infinitely many solutions (x = 1, any y), but the system has only (1, 1).

choices.text: A parked car's distance from home

questions.correct_answer: A parked car's distance from home
questions.grading_note: A parked car does not move.

questions.set_title: Sketch graphs that show key features given in a verbal description
questions.section_title: Sketch a graph from a description
questions.question: A graph that rises and then falls has a highest point.
questions.grading_note: It changes from increasing to decreasing at a maximum.

questions.set_title: Sketch graphs that show key features given in a verbal description
questions.section_title: Sketch a graph from a description
questions.question: A horizontal segment on a speed-time graph means the car is stopped.
questions.grading_note: It means the speed is constant, which may not be 0.

questions.set_title: Sketch graphs that show key features given in a verbal description
questions.section_title: Write and graph equations on labeled axes
questions.question: Write an equation for the area A of a square with side s. What kind of graph does it have for s ≥ 0?
questions.correct_answer: A = s²; half of a parabola, starting at (0, 0) and curving upward
questions.grading_note: Form required: the equation and the shape.

questions.set_title: Sketch graphs that show key features given in a verbal description
questions.section_title: Write and graph equations on labeled axes
questions.question: Graph C = 5 + 2n, the cost in dollars of a ride with n stops, for n = 0 to 5.
questions.correct_answer: Points (or a line) from (0, 5) to (5, 15), rising by 2 for each stop
questions.grading_note: Any correct graph; separate points are expected because n is a whole number.

questions.set_title: Sketch graphs that show key features given in a verbal description
questions.section_title: Write and graph equations on labeled axes
questions.question: A $1,200 laptop loses $200 of value each year. Which equation gives its value V after t years?
questions.grading_note: Start at 1,200 and subtract 200 per year.

questions.set_title: Sketch graphs that show key features given in a verbal description
questions.section_title: Write and graph equations on labeled axes
questions.question: An equation in two variables can be graphed on a coordinate plane.
questions.grading_note: Each solution is a point (x, y).

questions.set_title: Sketch graphs that show key features given in a verbal description
questions.section_title: Write and graph equations on labeled axes
questions.question: The graph of d = 50t is a curve.
questions.grading_note: It is a straight line through the origin with slope 50.

questions.set_title: Sketch graphs that show key features given in a verbal description
questions.section_title: Sketch polynomial graphs from a description of their features
questions.grade: High School — Algebra II (course placement in this bank)
questions.question: Sketch a cubic function that falls to the left, rises to the right, and has zeros at -2, 1, and 4. (The y-scale is up to you.)
questions.correct_answer: A curve crossing the x-axis at -2, 1, and 4, falling to the left and rising to the right, with one turn between -2 and 1 and one between 1 and 4
questions.grading_note: Any correct sketch, for example of y = (x + 2)(x - 1)(x - 4).

questions.set_title: Sketch graphs that show key features given in a verbal description
questions.section_title: Sketch polynomial graphs from a description of their features
questions.grade: High School — Algebra II (course placement in this bank)
questions.question: A polynomial graph touches the x-axis at x = 3 and turns around there. What can you say about the factor x - 3?
questions.correct_answer: It appears an even number of times, for example (x - 3)².
questions.grading_note: Any equivalent explanation (even multiplicity).

questions.set_title: Sketch graphs that show key features given in a verbal description
questions.section_title: Sketch polynomial graphs from a description of their features
questions.grade: High School — Algebra II (course placement in this bank)
questions.question: Which polynomial function has a graph that falls on both ends?
questions.grading_note: Even degree with a negative leading coefficient.

questions.set_title: Sketch graphs that show key features given in a verbal description
questions.section_title: Sketch polynomial graphs from a description of their features
questions.grade: High School — Algebra II (course placement in this bank)
questions.question: The graph of a degree-5 polynomial with a positive leading coefficient rises to the right.
questions.grading_note: Odd degree, positive leading coefficient: falls left, rises right.

questions.set_title: Sketch graphs that show key features given in a verbal description
questions.section_title: Sketch polynomial graphs from a description of their features
questions.grade: High School — Algebra II (course placement in this bank)
questions.question: The graph of a cubic function can rise on both ends.
questions.grading_note: A cubic rises on one end and falls on the other.

questions.set_title: Sketch graphs that show key features given in a verbal description
questions.section_title: Sketch periodic graphs from a description
questions.grade: High School — Algebra II (course placement in this bank)
questions.question: A Ferris wheel seat starts at its lowest height, 2 m, reaches its highest height, 42 m, after 5 minutes, and repeats every 10 minutes. Sketch its height over 20 minutes.
questions.correct_answer: A smooth wave starting at (0, 2), up to (5, 42), down to (10, 2), up to (15, 42), down to (20, 2), with midline 22
questions.grading_note: Any correct sketch with the minimum 2, maximum 42, period 10, and starting point.

questions.set_title: Sketch graphs that show key features given in a verbal description
questions.section_title: Sketch periodic graphs from a description
questions.grade: High School — Algebra II (course placement in this bank)
questions.question: Daylight lasts 15 hours in late June and 9 hours in late December. Describe a graph of daylight hours over a year.
questions.correct_answer: A wave with maximum 15 (June), minimum 9 (December), midline 12, and period 12 months.
questions.grading_note: Form required: the maximum, minimum, midline, and period.

questions.set_title: Sketch graphs that show key features given in a verbal description
questions.section_title: Sketch periodic graphs from a description
questions.grade: High School — Algebra II (course placement in this bank)
questions.question: Which feature of a periodic graph is the time for one full cycle?
questions.grading_note: The period is the length of one cycle.

questions.set_title: Sketch graphs that show key features given in a verbal description
questions.section_title: Sketch periodic graphs from a description
questions.grade: High School — Algebra II (course placement in this bank)
questions.question: The midline of a periodic graph is halfway between its maximum and minimum values.
questions.grading_note: Midline = (maximum + minimum) ÷ 2.

questions.set_title: Sketch graphs that show key features given in a verbal description
questions.section_title: Sketch periodic graphs from a description
questions.grade: High School — Algebra II (course placement in this bank)
questions.question: A tide graph that repeats every 12.4 hours has amplitude 12.4.
questions.grading_note: 12.4 hours is the period; the amplitude is a height.

questions.set_title: Relate the domain of a function to the quantity it describes
questions.section_title: Algebra I main question
questions.question: n(k) = 12k gives the number of eggs in k full cartons. The store has 30 cartons. What is a reasonable domain?
questions.grading_note: Form required: the domain, stated as whole numbers from 0 to 30.

questions.set_title: Relate the domain of a function to the quantity it describes
questions.section_title: Algebra I main question
questions.question: h(t) = -16t² + 64t gives a ball's height in feet from the moment it is hit until it lands. What is the domain?
questions.grading_note: Form required: an inequality (or interval). h(t) = -16t(t - 4) = 0 at t = 0 and t = 4.

questions.set_title: Relate the domain of a function to the quantity it describes
questions.section_title: Algebra I main question
questions.question: A taxi fare is C(m) = 3 + 2.5m dollars for m miles, with a limit of 40 miles per ride. What is the domain?
questions.grading_note: The input is miles, from 0 to the 40-mile limit. 3 ≤ C ≤ 103 is the range.

questions.set_title: Relate the domain of a function to the quantity it describes
questions.section_title: Algebra I main question
questions.question: A rectangle has perimeter 20. Its area is A(w) = w(10 - w), where w is the width. What is the domain?
questions.grading_note: Form required: an inequality. Both w and the length 10 - w must be positive.

questions.set_title: Relate the domain of a function to the quantity it describes
questions.section_title: Algebra I main question
questions.question: P(n) = 50n gives the number of seats on n buses. n = 2.5 is in a reasonable domain.
questions.grading_note: The number of buses must be a whole number.

questions.set_title: Relate the domain of a function to the quantity it describes
questions.section_title: Decide whether a solution is viable
questions.question: Solving a problem gives 7.4 buses needed to carry every student. What is the viable answer? Explain.
questions.correct_answer: 8 buses: the number must be a whole number, and 7 buses are not enough.
questions.grading_note: Form required: the number and a reason.

questions.set_title: Relate the domain of a function to the quantity it describes
questions.section_title: Decide whether a solution is viable
questions.question: The number of tickets t must satisfy 5t ≤ 60 and t ≥ 0. What whole numbers of tickets are viable?
questions.grading_note: Any equivalent form, such as the whole numbers from 0 to 12.

questions.set_title: Relate the domain of a function to the quantity it describes
questions.section_title: Decide whether a solution is viable
questions.question: Which value is NOT viable for the number of people in a room?
questions.grading_note: A count cannot be negative.

questions.set_title: Relate the domain of a function to the quantity it describes
questions.section_title: Decide whether a solution is viable
questions.question: A length of 0.25 meter can be a viable solution.
questions.grading_note: Lengths can be fractions.

questions.set_title: Relate the domain of a function to the quantity it describes
questions.section_title: Decide whether a solution is viable
questions.question: w(10 - w) = 24 has solutions w = 4 and w = 6, but only one of them is a viable width.
questions.grading_note: Both are viable: width 4 with length 6, or width 6 with length 4.

questions.set_title: Relate the domain of a function to the quantity it describes
questions.section_title: Find where a quadratic model equals 0
questions.question: Solve -16t² + 64t = 0.
questions.grading_note: Form required: both solutions. -16t(t - 4) = 0.

questions.set_title: Relate the domain of a function to the quantity it describes
questions.section_title: Find where a quadratic model equals 0
questions.question: Solve w(10 - w) = 0.
questions.grading_note: Form required: both solutions.

questions.set_title: Relate the domain of a function to the quantity it describes
questions.section_title: Find where a quadratic model equals 0
questions.question: Solve -16t² + 64t + 80 = 0.

questions.set_title: Relate the domain of a function to the quantity it describes
questions.section_title: Find where a quadratic model equals 0
questions.question: t = 4 is a solution of t² - 4t = 0.

questions.set_title: Relate the domain of a function to the quantity it describes
questions.section_title: Find where a quadratic model equals 0
questions.question: x² + 9 = 0 has two real solutions.
questions.grading_note: x² = -9 has no real solution.

questions.question: Right triangle ABC has its right angle at C, with AC = 4, BC = 3, and AB = 5. Find sin A.
questions.grading_note: Any equivalent form, such as 0.6. sin A = opposite ÷ hypotenuse = BC ÷ AB.

questions.section_title: Use trigonometric ratios as functions of acute angles
questions.grade: High School — Geometry (course placement in this bank)
questions.question: For which angle measures θ is sin θ defined as a ratio of sides of a right triangle?
questions.grading_note: Form required: an inequality. Only the acute angles of a right triangle are used.

questions.set_title: Relate the domain of a function to the quantity it describes
questions.section_title: Use trigonometric ratios as functions of acute angles
questions.grade: High School — Geometry (course placement in this bank)
questions.question: In a right triangle, cos A = 12/13. What is sin A?
questions.grading_note: The sides are 5, 12, 13, so the opposite side is 5.

questions.set_title: Relate the domain of a function to the quantity it describes
questions.section_title: Use trigonometric ratios as functions of acute angles
questions.grade: High School — Geometry (course placement in this bank)
questions.question: In a right triangle, sin A = cos B when A and B are the two acute angles.
questions.grading_note: The side opposite A is adjacent to B.

questions.set_title: Relate the domain of a function to the quantity it describes
questions.section_title: Use trigonometric ratios as functions of acute angles
questions.grade: High School — Geometry (course placement in this bank)
questions.question: For an acute angle θ, sin θ can be greater than 1.
questions.grading_note: The opposite side is shorter than the hypotenuse.

questions.set_title: Relate the domain of a function to the quantity it describes
questions.section_title: Extend trigonometric functions to all real numbers with the unit circle
questions.grade: High School — Algebra II (course placement in this bank)
questions.question: Find cos π.
questions.grading_note: Any equivalent form. The point at angle π is (-1, 0).

questions.section_title: Extend trigonometric functions to all real numbers with the unit circle
questions.grade: High School — Algebra II (course placement in this bank)
questions.question: Find sin(3π ÷ 2).
questions.grading_note: Any equivalent form. The point is (0, -1).

questions.set_title: Relate the domain of a function to the quantity it describes
questions.section_title: Extend trigonometric functions to all real numbers with the unit circle
questions.grade: High School — Algebra II (course placement in this bank)
questions.question: With the unit circle, what is the domain of f(θ) = sin θ?
questions.grading_note: Any real number of radians, positive or negative, gives a point on the unit circle.

questions.set_title: Relate the domain of a function to the quantity it describes
questions.section_title: Extend trigonometric functions to all real numbers with the unit circle
questions.grade: High School — Algebra II (course placement in this bank)
questions.question: A negative radian measure gives a clockwise rotation.
questions.grading_note: Positive angles turn counterclockwise.

questions.set_title: Relate the domain of a function to the quantity it describes
questions.section_title: Extend trigonometric functions to all real numbers with the unit circle
questions.grade: High School — Algebra II (course placement in this bank)
questions.question: sin θ is defined only for acute angles.
questions.grading_note: The unit circle defines it for every real number.

questions.set_title: Calculate, interpret, and estimate the average rate of change of a function over an interval
questions.section_title: Algebra I main question
questions.question: f(x) = x² + 2x. Find the average rate of change from x = 1 to x = 4.
questions.grading_note: Any equivalent form. (f(4) - f(1)) ÷ (4 - 1) = (24 - 3) ÷ 3.

questions.set_title: Calculate, interpret, and estimate the average rate of change of a function over an interval
questions.section_title: Algebra I main question
questions.question: A town had 12,000 people in 2010 and 15,600 in 2022. Find the average rate of change, with units.
questions.grading_note: Form required: the rate with its units. 3,600 ÷ 12 = 300.

questions.set_title: Calculate, interpret, and estimate the average rate of change of a function over an interval
questions.section_title: Algebra I main question
questions.question: The table gives the distance d a cart has traveled after t seconds. Over which 2-second interval was its average speed greatest? Give that speed.
questions.correct_answer: From t = 2 to t = 4, at 35 meters per second
questions.grading_note: Form required: the interval and the speed. The speeds are 15, 35, and 25 m/s.

questions.set_title: Calculate, interpret, and estimate the average rate of change of a function over an interval
questions.section_title: Algebra I main question
questions.question: What is the average rate of change of g(x) = 3^x from x = 0 to x = 2?

questions.set_title: Calculate, interpret, and estimate the average rate of change of a function over an interval
questions.section_title: Algebra I main question
questions.question: A linear function has the same average rate of change over every interval.
questions.grading_note: Its average rate of change is always its slope.

questions.set_title: Calculate, interpret, and estimate the average rate of change of a function over an interval
questions.section_title: Find the rate of change of a linear function
questions.question: Find the rate of change of the line through (2, 5) and (6, 17).
questions.grading_note: Any equivalent form. 12 ÷ 4.

questions.set_title: Calculate, interpret, and estimate the average rate of change of a function over an interval
questions.section_title: Find the rate of change of a linear function
questions.question: A tank had 50 liters at t = 0 and 20 liters at t = 10 minutes, draining steadily. What is the rate of change?
questions.grading_note: Any equivalent form, with units. (20 - 50) ÷ 10.

questions.set_title: Calculate, interpret, and estimate the average rate of change of a function over an interval
questions.section_title: Find the rate of change of a linear function
questions.question: What is the rate of change of y = 7 - 4x?
questions.grading_note: The coefficient of x is -4.

questions.set_title: Calculate, interpret, and estimate the average rate of change of a function over an interval
questions.section_title: Find the rate of change of a linear function
questions.question: A negative rate of change means the quantity is decreasing.
questions.grading_note: Outputs fall as inputs rise.

questions.set_title: Calculate, interpret, and estimate the average rate of change of a function over an interval
questions.section_title: Find the rate of change of a linear function
questions.question: The rate of change from (0, 3) to (2, 3) is 3.

questions.set_title: Calculate, interpret, and estimate the average rate of change of a function over an interval
questions.section_title: Compute unit rates with fractions
questions.question: A runner goes 3/4 mile in 1/8 hour. What is the speed in miles per hour?
questions.grading_note: Any equivalent form. {3/4} ÷ {1/8} = 6.

questions.set_title: Calculate, interpret, and estimate the average rate of change of a function over an interval
questions.section_title: Compute unit rates with fractions
questions.question: A car uses 12 gallons to go 300 miles. How many miles per gallon?
questions.grading_note: Any equivalent form.

questions.set_title: Calculate, interpret, and estimate the average rate of change of a function over an interval
questions.section_title: Compute unit rates with fractions
questions.question: A recipe uses 2/3 cup of sugar for 1/3 of a batch. How much sugar is used per batch?

questions.set_title: Calculate, interpret, and estimate the average rate of change of a function over an interval
questions.section_title: Compute unit rates with fractions
questions.question: 120 km in 1.5 hours is 80 km per hour.

questions.set_title: Calculate, interpret, and estimate the average rate of change of a function over an interval
questions.section_title: Compute unit rates with fractions
questions.question: $18 for 4 pounds is $4 per pound.
questions.grading_note: 18 ÷ 4 = $4.50 per pound.

questions.set_title: Calculate, interpret, and estimate the average rate of change of a function over an interval
questions.section_title: Build a periodic model from amplitude, period, and midline
questions.grade: High School — Algebra II (course placement in this bank)
questions.question: A Ferris wheel has diameter 40 m, its center is 25 m above the ground, and it turns once every 8 minutes. A rider starts at the lowest point. Write a model h(t) = A cos(Bt) + D for the rider's height after t minutes.
questions.grading_note: Any equivalent form. Amplitude 20, midline 25, B = 2π ÷ 8 = π ÷ 4; A is negative because the ride starts at the lowest point.

questions.set_title: Calculate, interpret, and estimate the average rate of change of a function over an interval
questions.section_title: Build a periodic model from amplitude, period, and midline
questions.grade: High School — Algebra II (course placement in this bank)
questions.question: h(t) = -20cos(πt ÷ 4) + 25 gives a rider's height in meters after t minutes. Give the amplitude, the period, and the midline.
questions.correct_answer: Amplitude 20 m; period 8 minutes; midline h = 25
questions.grading_note: Form required: all three. 2π ÷ (π ÷ 4) = 8.

questions.set_title: Calculate, interpret, and estimate the average rate of change of a function over an interval
questions.section_title: Build a periodic model from amplitude, period, and midline
questions.grade: High School — Algebra II (course placement in this bank)
questions.question: Daily high temperatures in a town vary from a low of 4 °C to a high of 28 °C over a 365-day year. Which values fit a sinusoidal model?
questions.grading_note: Amplitude (28 - 4) ÷ 2 = 12; midline (28 + 4) ÷ 2 = 16; one cycle per year.

questions.set_title: Calculate, interpret, and estimate the average rate of change of a function over an interval
questions.section_title: Build a periodic model from amplitude, period, and midline
questions.grade: High School — Algebra II (course placement in this bank)
questions.question: A model y = A cos(Bt) + D with period 12 hours has B = π ÷ 6.
questions.grading_note: 2π ÷ B = 12 gives B = π ÷ 6.

questions.set_title: Calculate, interpret, and estimate the average rate of change of a function over an interval
questions.section_title: Build a periodic model from amplitude, period, and midline
questions.grade: High School — Algebra II (course placement in this bank)
questions.question: A tide that rises from 1 m to 5 m and falls back again has amplitude 4 m.
questions.grading_note: The amplitude is half the distance from low to high: (5 - 1) ÷ 2 = 2 m.

questions.grade: High School — Precalculus (course placement in this bank)
questions.question: f(x) = 12 ÷ x. Find the average rate of change from x = 2 to x = 6.
questions.grading_note: Any equivalent form. (2 - 6) ÷ (6 - 2).

questions.set_title: Calculate, interpret, and estimate the average rate of change of a function over an interval
questions.section_title: Analyze rational functions: rates of change and asymptotes
questions.grade: High School — Precalculus (course placement in this bank)
questions.question: Give the vertical and horizontal asymptotes of f(x) = 1 ÷ (x - 3) + 2.
questions.grading_note: Form required: both asymptotes.

questions.set_title: Calculate, interpret, and estimate the average rate of change of a function over an interval

questions.question: Where is f(x) = (x + 1) ÷ (x - 4) undefined?
questions.grading_note: The denominator is 0 at x = 4.

questions.set_title: Calculate, interpret, and estimate the average rate of change of a function over an interval
questions.section_title: Analyze rational functions: rates of change and asymptotes
questions.grade: High School — Precalculus (course placement in this bank)
questions.question: The graph of y = 1 ÷ x gets closer to the x-axis as x gets large.
questions.grading_note: 1 ÷ x approaches 0.

questions.set_title: Calculate, interpret, and estimate the average rate of change of a function over an interval
questions.section_title: Analyze rational functions: rates of change and asymptotes
questions.grade: High School — Precalculus (course placement in this bank)
questions.question: Graph f(x) = 1 ÷ (x - 2) + 1. Draw both asymptotes as lines and mark the intercepts.
questions.correct_answer: Vertical asymptote x = 2 and horizontal asymptote y = 1; the curve passes through the x-intercept (1, 0) and the y-intercept (0, 0.5), with one branch below and left of (2, 1) and one above and right
questions.grading_note: Any correct graph. 1 ÷ (x - 2) = -1 gives x = 1; f(0) = -0.5 + 1 = 0.5.

questions.set_title: Estimate the average rate of change of a function from its graph
questions.section_title: Algebra I main question
questions.question: The graph shows the distance d, in meters, that a cart has rolled after t seconds. Estimate the average rate of change from t = 1 to t = 3, with units.
questions.grading_note: Form required: an estimate with units. Accept 3.5 to 4.5 m/s: the graph passes about (1, 1) and (3, 9), and (9 - 1) ÷ 2 = 4.

questions.set_title: Estimate the average rate of change of a function from its graph
questions.section_title: Algebra I main question
questions.question: The graph shows the distance d, in meters, that a cart has rolled after t seconds. Estimate the average rate of change from t = 3 to t = 5. Is the cart speeding up?
questions.correct_answer: About 8 meters per second; yes, the rate is greater than on earlier intervals.
questions.grading_note: Form required: an estimate (7 to 9 m/s) and the conclusion. (25 - 9) ÷ 2 = 8.

questions.set_title: Estimate the average rate of change of a function from its graph

questions.question: The graph shows the temperature of a cup of coffee. Estimate the average rate of change of the temperature over the first 5 minutes, with units.
questions.grading_note: Form required: an estimate with units. Accept -7 to -9 °C per minute: from about 80 °C to about 40 °C in 5 minutes.

questions.set_title: Estimate the average rate of change of a function from its graph
questions.section_title: Algebra I main question
questions.question: The graph shows the temperature of a cup of coffee. Over which 2-minute interval is the coffee cooling fastest on average?

questions.set_title: Estimate the average rate of change of a function from its graph

questions.grading_note: The average rate of change is the slope of the secant line: 36 ÷ 6 = 6 m/s.

questions.grade: High School — Probability & Statistics (course placement in this bank)
questions.domain: Statistics & Probability: Making Inferences & Justifying Conclusions
questions.question: Observational data show r = -0.6 between evening screen time and hours of sleep. To test cause, 50 volunteers were randomly assigned to no screens after 8 p.m. or to their usual habits. The no-screen group slept 0.5 hour more on average. In 1,000 random regroupings, a difference of at least 0.5 hour (no-screen minus usual) happened 2 times. Using a 5% threshold, is the difference significant? Explain.
questions.correct_answer: Yes. 2 ÷ 1,000 = 0.2%, which is below 5%, so chance alone is very unlikely to explain it; cutting evening screens likely increased sleep for volunteers like these.
questions.grading_note: Form required: the decision with the simulated proportion compared with 5%.

questions.question: Why can this randomized experiment, but not the observational correlation alone, support the claim that evening screens reduce sleep?
questions.correct_answer: Random assignment tends to balance other variables (such as stress or age) between the groups, so a significant difference can be credited to the treatment; in observational data a lurking variable could explain the correlation.
questions.grading_note: Any equivalent explanation that contrasts random assignment with possible lurking variables.
